message.content:
Let

\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{100}2^{-\left\lfloor 101k/j\right\rfloor}.
\]

For fixed \(j\), write \(k=r+jt\), where \(1\le r\le j\) and \(t\ge 0\). Then

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{101k}{j}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor \frac{101(r+jt)}{j}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor \frac{101r}{j}\right\rfloor+101t.
\]

Thus

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-\lfloor 101k/j\rfloor}
=
\frac{\sum_{r=1}^{j}2^{-\lfloor 101r/j\rfloor}}{1-2^{-101}}.
\]

So

\[
S=\frac{T}{1-2^{-101}},
\qquad
T=\sum_{j=1}^{100}\sum_{r=1}^{j}2^{-\lfloor 101r/j\rfloor}.
\]

Now collect coefficients in \(T\). Let \(c_n\) be the coefficient of \(2^{-n}\). Since \(1\le r\le j\le 100\), the possible values of \(\lfloor 101r/j\rfloor\) are \(1,2,\dots,101\).

For \(1\le n\le 99\), for a fixed \(j\), we need an integer \(r\) satisfying

\[
\frac{n j}{101}\le r<\frac{(n+1)j}{101}.
\]

Both endpoints are non-integers, and the interval length is \(j/101<1\). Therefore such an \(r\) exists iff

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{(n+1)j}{101}\right\rfloor-
\left\lfloor \frac{n j}{101}\right\rfloor=1.
\]

Hence

\[
c_n=\sum_{j=1}^{100}
\left(
\left\lfloor \frac{(n+1)j}{101}\right\rfloor-
\left\lfloor \frac{n j}{101}\right\rfloor
\right).
\]

Using the standard floor-sum identity

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{100}\left\lfloor \frac{a j}{101}\right\rfloor
=
50(a-1),\qquad 1\le a\le 100,
\]

we get

\[
c_n=50n-50(n-1)=50.
\]

Also,

\[
c_{100}=0,\qquad c_{101}=100,
\]

because \(\lfloor 101r/j\rfloor=101\) occurs exactly when \(r=j\).

Therefore

\[
T=50\sum_{n=1}^{99}2^{-n}+100\cdot 2^{-101}.
\]

Since

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{99}2^{-n}=1-2^{-99},
\]

we have

\[
T=50(1-2^{-99})+100\cdot 2^{-101}
=50-\frac{25}{2^{99}}.
\]

Thus

\[
S=\frac{50-\frac{25}{2^{99}}}{1-2^{-101}}
=
\frac{50\cdot 2^{101}-100}{2^{101}-1}
=
\frac{50(2^{101}-2)}{2^{101}-1}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{50(2^{101}-2)}{2^{101}-1}}
\]
